225.title: Barabbas (Mark 15:1–15)
225.hook: the crowd chooses a rebel over Jesus
225.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday and Good Friday many churches read the passion aloud with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so that everyone says crucify him and remembers that the crowd's failure can be anyone's.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rooster crowed twice in a courtyard, and your line was he wept. Did you let an old failure be honestly sad for a moment? Day two hundred twenty-five.

Think of the last time you watched a pile-on. A comment section, a group chat, a hallway. One person says something, a few more join in, and within minutes a whole crowd is certain. Nobody quite remembers how it started, and nobody wants to be the one who says, wait. Early in the morning, the council binds Jesus and hands him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, because only Rome can carry out an execution. Pilate asks him: are you the King of the Jews? Jesus answers, thou sayest it, and then goes silent again, and Pilate marvels. Outside, a crowd is gathering.
screen: `A PILE-ON.` → `HANDED OVER TO PILATE.` → `A CROWD GATHERS.`

segments.voice: Mark says that at the feast, the governor used to release one prisoner, whoever the people asked for. It's worth saying plainly: no record outside the Gospels mentions this custom, and historians aren't sure how it worked. In prison there's a man called Barabbas, held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising. Pilate asks the crowd: will you have me release the King of the Jews? Mark adds that Pilate knew the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy. And then, Mark says, the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas instead. Here's the detail that stops scholars in their tracks. Barabbas is an Aramaic name: bar abba, son of the father. Remember abba, from the garden, two days ago? Jesus called God abba. Now the crowd is offered two men: one called son of the father, and one Christians call the Son of the Father. And some old copies of Matthew's Gospel even give the rebel's first name as Jesus. So Pilate asks, what then shall I do with him? Crucify him, they shout. Why, what evil hath he done? They shout louder. And Mark says, in the King James Bible: "And so Pilate, willing to content the people, released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus, when he had scourged him, to be crucified." Willing to content the people. The most powerful man in the province does what the loudest voices want. The crowd was a crowd that morning, stirred up by a few, and it was wrong. Christians have long heard something else in it too: the guilty man walks free, and the innocent one takes his place.
screen: `ONE PRISONER RELEASED AT THE FEAST.` · `BAR ABBA: SON OF THE FATHER.` · `CRUCIFY HIM.` · `WILLING TO CONTENT THE PEOPLE.` · then, large: `RELEASED BARABBAS UNTO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold in mind the crowds who get it wrong. Settle, and breathe. Think of a crowd you've seen lately turn on someone: online, at work, in the news. Picture the people in it, one by one, just ordinary people caught up in the noise. And picture the one they're shouting at. If you pray, you can pray for both: for the crowd, and for the person in the middle. If you don't, simply wish them all a quieter heart. The bell holds the time.
Barabbas. Bar abba, son of the father: the rebel the crowd chose to set free instead of Jesus.

Your line: the crowd isn't always right. Today, when you feel a crowd pulling you toward certainty about someone, be the one who pauses and asks, wait, what did he actually do? Day two hundred twenty-five.

226.title: The crown of thorns (Mark 15:16–32)
226.hook: soldiers mock; Simon of Cyrene carries the cross; passers-by jeer
226.howItsDone: Many Christians walk the Stations of the Cross, especially on Fridays in Lent, stopping to remember moments like the crown of thorns and Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barabbas went free, and your line was the crowd isn't always right. Did you pause when a crowd pulled you? Day two hundred twenty-six.

The soldiers lead Jesus into the governor's courtyard and call together the whole company. And they put on a show. They dress him in purple, the color of emperors. They twist a crown out of thorns and press it on his head. They salute him: hail, King of the Jews! They strike his head with a reed, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. It's the kind of cruelty bored, powerful people invent when someone can't fight back. When they've had their fun, they strip off the purple, put his own clothes back on him, and lead him out to crucify him.
screen: `THE WHOLE COMPANY, CALLED TOGETHER.` → `PURPLE, AND A CROWN OF THORNS.` → `HAIL, KING OF THE JEWS.`

segments.voice: On the road out of the city, the soldiers grab a man coming in from the country, Simon of Cyrene, and make him carry the cross. Mark adds a detail nobody needed: Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus. Why name the sons? Most likely because Mark's first readers knew them. A stranger pressed into service, and his family remembered it. They come to Golgotha, which Mark translates for us: the place of a skull. They offer him wine mixed with myrrh, and he doesn't take it. They crucify him, and divide his clothes by casting lots. Above his head, the charge: the King of the Jews. Two rebels are crucified with him, one on each side. Then the mocking starts again, and it comes from everyone. People walking past shake their heads: you who would destroy the temple, save yourself! The chief priests and scribes say to each other, in the King James Bible: "He saved others; himself he cannot save." Even the men crucified beside him join in. Here's the strange thing. The mockers keep saying things that, to Mark's readers, are true. They call him king in mockery; Christians call him king. They say he saved others; Mark has spent fifteen chapters showing just that: a leper, a little girl, a man in the tombs. And the jeer, himself he cannot save, is, for Christians, close to the whole point. He doesn't come down, not because he can't, but because saving others is what he's doing. The mockers get the words right and the meaning upside down.
screen: `SIMON OF CYRENE CARRIES THE CROSS.` · `GOLGOTHA: THE PLACE OF A SKULL.` · `THE CHARGE: THE KING OF THE JEWS.` · `THE MOCKERS SAY TRUE THINGS.` · then, large: `HE SAVED OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with someone mocked. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's the butt of the joke right now: a kid at school, a coworker everyone rolls their eyes at, a stranger online. Picture their face. Then picture Simon, a man who happened to be walking by, who ended up carrying the weight. What would it look like to walk alongside that person for a bit? One kind word, one seat next to them. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
The crown of thorns. The soldiers' cruel joke, a king's crown made of thorns, and the words hail, King of the Jews.

Your line: he saved others. Today, when you hear someone being mocked, don't join in. Be a little like Simon: carry some of the weight, even if you just happened to be walking by. Day two hundred twenty-six.

227.title: Why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:33–41)
227.hook: he cries the first line of Psalm 22, and a Roman soldier says: truly the Son of God; the women watch
227.howItsDone: Many churches hold a service on Good Friday afternoon, often around the ninth hour, and some pray Psalm 22 or meditate on the last words of Jesus from all four Gospels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crown of thorns and a crowd of mockers, and your line was he saved others. Did you carry a little weight for someone? Day two hundred twenty-seven.

Some of the hardest words anyone says are the ones they say at a hospital bedside, at 3am, when no answer comes. Why? Where are you? Mark doesn't soften what happens next. At the sixth hour, around noon, darkness covers the whole land until the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon. And at the ninth hour, Jesus cries out with a loud voice. Mark gives us the words in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, and then translates them. It is the only saying from the cross in all of Mark.
screen: `DARKNESS AT NOON.` → `THE NINTH HOUR.` → `A LOUD CRY.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those words weren't new. They're the opening line of Psalm 22, a prayer Jesus would have known by heart. The psalm starts in anguish: surrounded, mocked, bones out of joint, enemies dividing his garments. And it ends in trust: the psalmist praising God in the great congregation. Christians read the cry in different ways, and they sit together. Some hear real abandonment, the Son going all the way down into the silence people feel when God seems gone. Others point out that in his time you could call up a whole psalm by its first line, so he may be praying all of Psalm 22, including its ending. Many hold both. Either way, it matters that the prayer of the dying Jesus is a question. Some bystanders mishear: he's calling Elijah! One runs to give him sour wine on a sponge. Then Jesus gives a loud cry and breathes his last. At that moment, Mark says, the curtain of the temple is torn in two, from top to bottom. And the Roman centurion standing facing him, the soldier in charge of the execution, says: "Truly this man was the Son of God." Mark's gospel opened by calling Jesus the Son of God. Now, at the end, the first person to say it out loud is a Roman soldier. And watching from a distance: the women. Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome, and many others who had followed him from Galilee. The men had fled. The women stayed.
screen: `ELOI, ELOI, LAMA SABACHTHANI?` · `THE FIRST LINE OF PSALM 22.` · `THE CURTAIN TORN, TOP TO BOTTOM.` · `THE WOMEN WATCHED.` · then, large: `TRULY THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Psalm 22. If you can, open it now, in any Bible, and read it slowly, all the way through. Notice where it's darkest, and notice where it turns. If you can't open it, just sit with its first line: my God, my God, why? And think of someone who is asking that question right now. You don't need an answer for them. The women didn't have one either. They just stayed. The bell holds the time.
Why have you forsaken me? The only words Jesus speaks from the cross in Mark: the first line of Psalm 22, cried aloud in Aramaic.
screen: `WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the women stayed. Today, when someone near you is going through something you can't fix, don't leave because you don't know what to say. Just stay. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

228.title: Joseph of Arimathea (Mark 15:42–47)
228.hook: a council member boldly asks for the body and lays it in a tomb
228.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday many churches keep a quiet day of waiting by the tomb; Orthodox Christians carry an embroidered cloth of the burial in procession, and Joseph of Arimathea is honored with a feast day in several churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cry from the cross, the first line of Psalm 22, and your line was the women stayed. Did you stay with someone, even without words? Day two hundred twenty-eight.

When someone dies, somebody has to do the practical things. Call the family. Sign the forms. Pick the clothes. It's the least glamorous kindness there is, and often the bravest. It's late afternoon on Friday. Jesus is dead. The disciples are gone. The Sabbath begins at sunset, and in Jewish law a body shouldn't be left hanging overnight. Under Roman custom, the bodies of crucified rebels were often left on the cross, or thrown in a common grave. Somebody has to ask for him. And the man who does is someone we've never met before.
screen: `FRIDAY, LATE AFTERNOON.` → `THE SABBATH COMING AT SUNSET.` → `SOMEBODY HAS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Mark introduces him in one breath, in the King James Bible: "Joseph of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus." Look at who he is. A counsellor: a member of the council, the same council that just condemned Jesus. Mark earlier said all of them condemned him; Luke adds that Joseph had not agreed with their decision. He's respected and he's comfortable. And he's waiting for the kingdom of God, which means he'd been listening. Then look at the verb. He went in boldly. The Greek word means he dared. Walking into the Roman governor's house to ask for the body of a man just executed as king of the Jews could cost him his standing, maybe more. He goes anyway. Pilate is surprised Jesus is already dead, calls the centurion to confirm it, and gives Joseph the body. Joseph buys fine linen, takes him down, wraps him, lays him in a tomb cut out of the rock, and rolls a stone against the door. And two people are watching: Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses. They see where he is laid. That detail matters for Sunday. Here's what's striking. The disciples, who knew him best, are nowhere. The one who shows up is a quiet insider who until now had kept his hopes to himself. Christians remember him as a patron of anyone who cares for the dead, and many churches honor him with a feast day. Sometimes courage is loud. Sometimes it's a respectable man asking an awkward question, and then doing the heavy lifting himself.
screen: `A COUNCILLOR, WAITING FOR THE KINGDOM.` · `HE DARED: HE WENT IN BOLDLY.` · `LINEN, ROCK AND A ROLLED STONE.` · `THE TWO MARYS SEE WHERE.` · then, large: `AND CRAVED THE BODY OF JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a brave kindness for someone gone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has died: a grandparent, a friend, someone you barely knew. What's one kindness you could still do for them? Visit their grave. Call the person they left behind. Tell their story to someone who never met them. Pick the one that feels a little awkward, the one that takes a bit of daring. If you pray, you can remember them before God. The bell holds the time.
Joseph of Arimathea. The council member who dared to ask Pilate for the body of Jesus, and laid him in a tomb cut in the rock.
Your line: he went in boldly. Today, do the kindness that makes you a little nervous: the call, the visit, the question nobody else wants to ask. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

229.title: Trembling and astonishment (Mark 16:1–8)
229.hook: the women find the tomb empty; the oldest copies end with them fleeing, afraid
229.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the resurrection every Easter and every Sunday; many churches hold sunrise services on Easter morning, and Orthodox Christians greet each other with Christ is risen, answered, he is risen indeed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a councillor who dared to ask for the body, and your line was he went in boldly. Did you do the kindness that made you nervous? Day two hundred twenty-nine.

The Sabbath is over. Very early on Sunday morning, as the sun is coming up, three women walk to the tomb: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. They've bought spices to anoint his body, the last thing they can do for him. And on the way they're worried about something very practical. Who will roll away the stone for us? It's huge. They'd watched it go in. Then they look up. The stone is already rolled back.
screen: `VERY EARLY, THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `WHO WILL ROLL AWAY THE STONE?` → `IT'S ALREADY ROLLED BACK.`

segments.voice: They go into the tomb, and sitting on the right side is a young man in a long white robe. They are terrified. And he says, in the King James Bible: "Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him." Then he gives them a message: go, tell his disciples, and Peter, that he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he said. And Peter. Of all the names to single out, it's the one who denied him three times by the fire. Then comes the last verse of Mark in the oldest copies we have: "And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid." That's it. No appearance of the risen Jesus. No reunion. Just women running from an empty tomb, shaking. In Greek, the end of the sentence is literally, they were afraid, for. It ends on a small word, gar, like a sentence cut off mid-breath. Scholars have argued about this for centuries. Maybe the last page was lost. Maybe Mark meant to stop here. If he did, the ending is a kind of invitation: the story isn't finished; it hands the next step to whoever is reading. And we know the women didn't stay silent forever, or there'd be no story to read. The trembling and astonishment are the right response. Not calm, not neat: awe. In Greek, trembling is tromos, and astonishment is ekstasis, which gives English the word ecstasy. Something so big it takes you outside yourself.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN IN A WHITE ROBE.` · `TELL HIS DISCIPLES, AND PETER.` · `THEY WERE AFRAID, FOR.` · `TROMOS AND EKSTASIS.` · then, large: `HE IS RISEN; HE IS NOT HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with an ending that's also a beginning. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that ended: a job, a friendship, a season, a home. Let yourself feel what the women felt on that walk: the heaviness, the practical worries, who will roll away the stone. Then ask gently: what began after that ending, even if you didn't see it at the time? You don't need a neat answer. Just notice. If you pray, you can hold that ending before God. The bell holds the time.
Trembling and astonishment. What seized the women at the empty tomb, in the last verse of Mark's oldest copies: tromos and ekstasis.
Your line: he goes before you. Today, walk into one place you're dreading, and notice what's already been done before you get there. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

230.title: The longer ending (Mark 16:9–20)
230.hook: later verses add appearances and a commission; scholars note it wasn't in the earliest manuscripts
230.howItsDone: The longer ending is read in Catholic and Orthodox services, often around the Ascension, and many Protestant Bibles print it with a note that the earliest manuscripts end at verse eight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an empty tomb and women who fled, trembling. Your line was he goes before you. What did you find already done when you got there? Day two hundred thirty.

If you open a Bible to the end of Mark, you might notice something odd. After verse eight, many modern Bibles put in a line or a bracket, or a small note: some of the earliest manuscripts end here. And then they keep going. Twelve more verses. If yesterday's ending left you hanging, the women running and afraid, then you're in good company. Very early on, Christians felt that too. And the church ended up with more than one way to finish the story.
screen: `A BRACKET AFTER VERSE EIGHT.` → `SOME MANUSCRIPTS END HERE.` → `TWELVE MORE VERSES.`

segments.voice: Here's what the longer ending says. The risen Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast seven devils. She tells the mourning disciples, and they don't believe her. He appears to two of them walking in the country; they tell the rest, and again nobody believes. Then he appears to the eleven at a meal, and scolds them for their unbelief and hardness of heart. And he gives them their commission, in the King James Bible: "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Then he is taken up into heaven, and they go out and preach everywhere. Now, the honest part. The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts of Mark, from the three hundreds, stop at verse eight. The vocabulary and style of these twelve verses are different from the rest of Mark. And the verses sound like a summary of appearances told in the other Gospels and Acts. So most scholars think they were added by a later hand. There's even a second, shorter ending in some manuscripts, just a sentence or two. But the longer ending is also very old. A church writer named Irenaeus seems to quote it well before the year two hundred, and it's in the vast majority of manuscripts. Churches hold it in different ways. The Catholic and Orthodox churches receive it as part of scripture, and it's read in their services. Many Protestant Bibles print it with a note. Almost everyone agrees on what it's doing: finishing the thought. Fear becomes a mission. The disciples who fled are sent out into all the world.
screen: `MARY MAGDALENE, FIRST.` · `THEY DID NOT BELIEVE.` · `NOT IN THE OLDEST COPIES.` · `CHURCHES HOLD IT IN DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `GO YE INTO ALL THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the ending and the added ending. If you can, open Mark 16 now. Read verses one to eight, slowly. Stop, and notice how it feels to end on they were afraid. Then read verses nine to twenty. Notice how it feels to end on a mission. You don't have to decide anything about manuscripts. Just notice what each ending does to you. If you pray, you can offer both, the fear and the going, to God. The bell holds the time.
The longer ending. Mark 16, verses nine to twenty: appearances, a commission and an ascension, missing from the oldest copies and very old all the same.
Your line: go into all the world. Today, take one thing you're afraid of and turn it into a small errand: one message sent, one step out the door. Day two hundred thirty.

231.title: Camp 4 close: back to Galilee
231.hook: the young man said: he's going ahead of you to Galilee, back where it all began (Mark 16:7)
231.howItsDone: Many churches read through one Gospel across a year of Sundays, and Mark is read in the second year of the shared three-year lectionary that Catholics and many Protestants use.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the longer ending of Mark, and your line was go into all the world. Did you turn one fear into a small errand? Day two hundred thirty-one. The end of the week, and the close of camp four.

Have you ever gone back to your hometown after something big happened? The streets are the same. The diner is the same. But you're not. You notice things you walked past a hundred times. At the empty tomb, the young man in white gave the women a message for the disciples. In the King James Bible: "he goeth before you into Galilee: there shall ye see him, as he said unto you." Not to Rome. Not to the temple. Back to Galilee. Back to the lake, the boats, the nets, the little towns where it all began.
screen: `BACK TO YOUR HOMETOWN.` → `HE GOETH BEFORE YOU INTO GALILEE.` → `WHERE IT ALL BEGAN.`

segments.voice: For seventy-five days, this camp has read one book, the Gospel of Mark, in order, a few verses at a time. Let's walk back through it. It began with a single line: the beginning of the good news. Then the heavens torn open, and fishermen told to leave the nets. Friends dug through a roof. A leper heard I am willing. A sower threw seed everywhere, and a man slept on a cushion in a storm. A little girl heard talitha koum, get up. Five thousand were fed, and a woman who was told she was a dog answered back, and won. At Caesarea Philippi came the question at the center of the book: who do you say I am? Then the road to Jerusalem: take up your cross; a blind man named Bartimaeus asked to see; a widow gave all she had. And in the last two weeks: perfume poured out, bread broken, abba in the garden, Peter weeping by the fire, a crown of thorns, the women who stayed, and an empty tomb. Now here's why Galilee matters. Mark's ending sends the disciples back to the beginning. Many readers think Mark means you, too, to go back to chapter one and read it again, knowing how it ends. The disciples misunderstood almost everything the first time through. Read again, the same stories look different. The very first verse, in the King James Bible, says: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning. As if the whole book is only the start. Tomorrow a new camp begins: camp five, the depths, and it opens with Jesus sitting down on a mountain to teach.
